headline: Maryland: medical 280E relief expected even without DEA registration
dek: Maryland's regulator said on 20 November that medical 280E relief should not depend on DEA registration, and flagged delta-8 as a DEA risk.
key_points: The Maryland Cannabis Administration's FAQ, updated 20 November, says state medical licensees are expected to escape Section 280E for the 2026 tax year whether or not they register with the DEA.
The regulator repeats that businesses choosing not to register with the DEA will face no action from the state, and it makes no recommendation either way.
It says Maryland's combined medical and adult-use licences, patient self-certification and the sale of delta-8 and delta-10 hemp products appear to be grounds the DEA cites in show cause orders.
Maryland is weighing split medical and adult-use licences and a way to share licensees' DEA status, but has committed to neither.
body: Maryland's cannabis regulator has told its licensees that the tax break from federal rescheduling should reach them even if they stay out of the DEA's registration system. In the second version of its Medical Cannabis Rescheduling Webinar FAQ, dated 20 November, the Maryland Cannabis Administration (MCA) says the federal order removes Section 280E's deduction ban from state medical marijuana licensees for the 2026 tax year, and that the benefit is expected to apply regardless of whether a business pursues registration. Further guidance from the Treasury is still to come, it adds.

The three-page document, first reported by The Marijuana Herald on 21 November, also confirms something the MCA said on 4 November: a Maryland business that decides not to register with the DEA will face no action from the state. It lands a week before the DEA's 29 November deadline for pending applicants to trade only with other applicants and registrants.

Section 280E bars businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II drugs from deducting ordinary expenses, which has meant cannabis companies pay federal income tax on gross profit rather than net income. Moving state medical marijuana to Schedule III takes those businesses outside the rule. The open question for many operators has been whether the relief depends on holding a DEA registration.

The MCA's answer is that it does not, at least for 2026, though it is careful to frame this as an expectation drawn from the federal order, not a ruling of its own. The FAQ opens with a warning that it is informational only, does not override Maryland or federal law, and may change as federal agencies act. The MCA also states plainly that it has no authority over federal rescheduling.
> Maryland is telling operators they can keep the tax break and skip the registration. The DEA's show cause orders suggest the registration route may be closed to many of them anyway.

The FAQ is blunt about the limits of rescheduling. It says the order covers FDA-approved drugs containing marijuana and marijuana held under a state medical licence by a DEA-registered entity. Adult-use cannabis and unlicensed bulk marijuana remain in Schedule I and subject to federal criminal law, and the MCA reminds licensees that Schedule III drugs carry federal restrictions and criminal penalties too.

State law is unchanged. Maryland investigators remain the main enforcers of state rules, and every licensee must keep complying with Maryland statutes and regulations. The MCA says it will issue an updated licence cover letter confirming a business's medical authorisation, which licensees can show the DEA if asked.
## Why Maryland businesses face show cause orders

The most consequential passage concerns the DEA's show cause orders, which the agency sent on 30 October to some applicants nationwide. The MCA says the grounds cited appear to be dual-use licensing, patient self-certification and allowing artificial or synthetic cannabinoids in the regulated market. It stresses that a show cause order starts an administrative proceeding and is not itself a denial.

All three grounds touch Maryland. The state runs a combined medical and adult-use licence structure. And when asked whether the tested delta-8 and delta-10 hemp products sold in Maryland dispensaries expose them to a show cause order, the MCA answered yes: the allowance of artificial and synthetic hemp-derived products appears to be grounds. That is an unusually direct admission from a state regulator that its own market rules may stand between its licensees and federal registration.

The MCA says it is evaluating options, including split medical and adult-use licences, to see how its dual structure can best withstand federal requirements, but has made no commitment. Conditional licensees, it adds, probably cannot register yet because the DEA application requires final state authorisation.

The FAQ recaps the federal timetable: the DEA portal accepted dispensary applications from 29 April to 26 June, and applicants who filed in that window were promised expedited review within six months. On 30 October the DEA sent timely applicant letters allowing pending applicants to keep operating under their state licences while their applications are reviewed.

Those timely applicants now need to find each other. The MCA says it is considering whether to collect licensees' DEA application status and registration numbers and share them with other licensees, but will decide only once the federal process for building supply chains among timely applicants is clearer. On interstate commerce, it says it has heard nothing from the FDA or other federal agencies and will wait for them before saying what is allowed.

The FAQ also explains the 'purchase and resale' mechanism growers have asked about: under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, the DEA must act as an intermediary buyer, purchasing crops at a nominal price and selling them back to the grower with an administrative fee.

On 23 November the government's response is due in the D.C. Circuit challenge to the DEA's 29 November deadline, as we reported on 21 November. On 29 November the deadline itself takes effect unless the court or the DEA moves it. Watch for Treasury guidance on how 280E relief will be claimed for 2026, for whether the MCA decides to publish licensees' DEA status, and for any move toward split licences, which would need changes to how Maryland's combined market is regulated.
